newsitem.title: GERMANY: German firms seek to shed light on Nazi past.
newsitem.headline: German firms seek to shed light on Nazi past.

text.p: Feeling an urgency to shed new light on less flattering parts of their history, several German firms are opening archives to researchers preparing books about the companies' role during the Nazi regime.

"We want clarity about our corporate history, and we will actively support this effort," Henning Schulte-Noelle, chief executive at Allianz AG, said on Friday in announcing the insurer had picked a U.S. historian to write a comprehensive new study about its history.

Launched over 50 years after the end of World War Two, these new projects are being hurried along at a time of intense public interest in and controversy over the role German groups played during the Third Reich.
Allianz, for example, is one of several insurers recently named in a multi-billion-dollar U.S. lawsuit that alleged Holocaust survivors were cheated of their assets.
Metals and chemicals group Degussa AG, is also preparing a new look at its history amid allegations it bought and melted down gold teeth and wedding rings taken from Holocaust victims.
"Our project is part of a general effort to shed more light on areas that have not been fully illuminated," Degussa spokesman Wolfgang Heilmann said.
But Heilmann noted the U.S. lawsuit sped up the process.

Allianz and Degussa will join national railway Deutsche Bahn AG, carmaker Volkswagen AG and Deutsche Bank AG, Germany's largest bank, in presenting a critical independent look at what their managers did to aid the Nazi war effort.

Key reasons for the new surge in self-examination range from a quest for stronger corporate identities to the publics' fascination with the Nazi years, said Andrea Schneider, chairwoman of the German Association for Corporate History.

"One main reason we are seeing companies tackle this part of history more boldly now is that there has been a change in management. The old guard, many of whom still had personal experiences with the Nazi era, are now gone, and one can take a less emotional look at those times," she said.

Deutsche Bank and Volkswagen, for example, ultimately received public praise for coming clean about how Germany's biggest bank profited from selling confiscated Jewish property and VW employed slave labour to build vehicles.

Hoping to capitalise on that success, Schneider's group is urging more German companies to expose their past with a two-day forum for historians and company executives to exchange ideas and make contacts for research projects.

"We will help companies find the appropriate historians to help them write their history," Schneider said, adding her list of contacts include renowned international historians who often commanded as much as one million marks for their studies.
After having come under fire for having earlier produced glamourised versions of their past, sometimes by in-house historians, companies said historians needed to be neutral.
"Picking someone neutral is very important, and we thought an American would be certainly by an outsider to this topic," Allianz's Heilmann said.

Conspicuously absent from the list are Germany's three leading chemical companies Hoechst AG, Bayer AG and BASF AG, formerly part of IG Farben, the maker of the Zyklon gas that Nazis used to kill Jews.
"We are trying to get them to join our group again, and they are considering it," Schneider said.
